Name: compute_buffer_tokens
Title: How Much Is Thinking Just Buffer Space? Measuring Serial-Computation Demand to Replace Verbose CoT with Minimal Contentless Compute Tokens
Short Hypothesis: A substantial fraction of chain-of-thought (CoT) accuracy gains comes not from the semantic content of reasoning text but from the extra serial forward passes it provides as scratchpad 'compute buffer.' If we can mechanistically estimate each problem's serial-computation demand, we can replace verbose CoT with a minimal, per-instance number of contentless compute-buffer tokens (e.g., repeated inert placeholder tokens) that recover most of the accuracy at a fraction of the tokens, without retraining for models that already exhibit filler-token benefits and with light adapter tuning for those that do not.
Related Work: Pfau et al. (2024, 'Let's Think Dot by Dot') showed transformers can solve certain tasks using meaningless filler tokens, but focused on constructed tasks with dedicated training and did not measure per-instance compute demand or build an efficient-reasoning controller. Latent/compressed-reasoning methods (Coconut, Heima, implicit CoT) replace explicit reasoning with learned continuous thoughts but require substantial retraining and give no interpretable, per-problem budget. Pause-token work (Goyal et al.) inserts a fixed number of learnable pause tokens uniformly, not adaptively. My prior proposals prune or skip content-bearing CoT; none ask whether the content matters at all versus the raw serial compute, nor estimate a per-instance compute-demand budget to allocate contentless buffer tokens. This proposal is distinct: it disentangles the 'content' vs 'compute buffer' contributions of CoT mechanistically and turns a serial-computation-demand estimate into an adaptive contentless-token efficiency method.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning accuracy, but it is unclear how much of that benefit stems from the semantic content of the generated text versus the extra serial computation the additional forward passes provide. We hypothesize that a large share of the gain is 'compute buffer': the model exploits the extra token positions as scratchpad depth, and much of the verbalized content is dispensable. We test this by comparing three conditions at matched token budgets: (1) full natural CoT, (2) content-scrambled CoT (semantically destroyed but structurally similar), and (3) contentless compute-buffer tokens (repeated inert placeholders). The gap between full CoT and scrambled/placeholder conditions estimates the content-specific contribution; the gap between no-thinking and placeholder conditions estimates the pure compute-buffer contribution. We then define a mechanistic, per-instance 'serial-computation demand': using logit-lens/probe convergence of the answer representation as a function of how many buffer tokens are inserted, we estimate the minimum number of buffer tokens after which the internal answer stabilizes. We build an adaptive controller that reads this demand from the prompt (via a lightweight probe) and allocates just enough contentless compute-buffer tokens per problem, then emits the answer. On GSM8K, MATH, and ProntoQA across DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen/Llama models (1.5B-8B), we report accuracy-vs-tokens Pareto curves against full CoT, fixed pause-token baselines, and truncation, expecting large token savings on problems whose gain is compute-driven, plus a mechanistic decomposition of what CoT tokens actually buy.
Experiments: 1. Content-vs-buffer decomposition: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, for GSM8K/MATH/ProntoQA compare four conditions at matched token counts: (a) full natural CoT, (b) content-scrambled CoT (shuffle words / replace with random on-vocabulary tokens preserving length and format), (c) contentless compute-buffer tokens (a repeated inert placeholder such as '.' or a reserved token), (d) direct answer (no thinking). Force answer emission after the same budget in each condition. Report accuracy per condition and per problem to decompose content-specific vs compute-buffer contributions. 2. Which models/tasks benefit from buffer alone: characterize the fraction of problems where placeholder tokens recover most of full-CoT accuracy, correlated with difficulty and CoT length; test whether models needing explicit training (light LoRA on placeholder-token reasoning) unlock the buffer benefit and by how much. 3. Serial-computation-demand estimate: for each problem, sweep the number of inserted buffer tokens and, using logit-lens/answer probe, find the buffer count after which the internal answer prediction stabilizes ('demand'); characterize demand distribution vs difficulty. 4. Adaptive controller: train a lightweight linear probe on final-prompt-token hidden states to predict per-instance buffer demand; at inference allocate that many contentless tokens then force the answer. 5. Evaluation: accuracy vs mean tokens generated (Pareto) and wall-clock latency; baselines: full CoT, fixed pause-token count (Goyal-style), fixed truncation, and direct answer. Metrics: accuracy, tokens, demand-probe error, per-difficulty accuracy breakdown. 6. Ablations: placeholder token choice, scrambling scheme, with/without light LoRA adaptation, layer choice for probe, cross-dataset and cross-model transfer of the demand probe, and interaction between compute-buffer allocation and residual content (short summary + buffer hybrid).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Many strong reasoning models may derive most benefit from content, not buffer, so placeholder recovery could be small without retraining; the decomposition quantifies this and the LoRA condition tests whether the buffer capacity can be unlocked cheaply. 2. Matching token budgets across conditions is subtle (scrambled vs placeholder vs natural lengths differ); we control by fixing the number of pre-answer positions. 3. Content-scrambling may inadvertently leave usable signal (numbers, format); we test multiple scrambling schemes including full random-token replacement. 4. Serial-computation demand may be poorly forecastable from the prompt for hard items, limiting adaptive savings; the probe-error and per-difficulty analyses define scope. 5. Placeholder-token benefits are known to be architecture/training dependent (Pfau et al.), so results may vary widely across models—this variation is itself an informative finding. 6. Probes/adapters may not transfer across models/datasets, requiring cheap one-time calibration; transfer is tested explicitly.
